questions.q: What does the Execute Package Task let a package do?
options: Convert a package to the project deployment model
Run a SQL Server Agent job
Run another SSIS package (a child package) as part of its own workflow
Restart the SSIS service
questions.explain: The Execute Package Task extends a package by letting it run another package — the child package — as a step in its own control flow.

questions.q: What does setting ReferenceType to Project Reference require?
options: Nothing extra — Project Reference works with any package location
The parent and child packages must share the same connection managers
The child package must be stored in the msdb database
The child package must be in the same project as the parent, using the project deployment model
questions.explain: Project Reference only works when the child package lives in the same project as the parent and that project uses the project deployment model; otherwise ReferenceType is locked to External Reference.

questions.q: What happens when ExecuteOutOfProcess is set to True?
options: The child package runs faster because it skips validation
The child package is prevented from writing to the log
The parent package can no longer pass parameters to the child
The child package runs in its own process, adding memory overhead but isolating failures from the parent
questions.explain: True runs the child package out-of-process — more memory and a slower launch, but a crash in the child doesn't necessarily crash the parent's process.

questions.q: How does logging behave between a parent and child package?
options: Only error-level log entries are forwarded
Logging never crosses between parent and child packages
The child package always forwards its log details to the parent, regardless of the child's own logging configuration
The parent's logging configuration overwrites the child's log entirely
questions.explain: Child packages always forward their log details up to the parent; if the Execute Package Task itself is configured to use logging, it logs those forwarded details too.

questions.q: Which is NOT a reason given for splitting a package into parent and child packages?
options: It breaks down complex workflow into readable, testable pieces
It lets you reuse a shared package from multiple parents
It lets you restrict package authors' access for security
It makes the package run on a faster CPU automatically
questions.explain: Splitting packages doesn't change CPU allocation — the real reasons are simplifying workflow, reusing packages, grouping transactional work units, and controlling security access.
